units.title: Distinguish plaque from calculus
units.lesson: Dental plaque is a bacterial biofilm on teeth. It can mineralize into calculus. Plaque and calculus are related but not interchangeable words: one is a biofilm, the other its hardened deposit. This distinction helps organize the causes of inflammation without treating every visible deposit as a complete periodontal diagnosis.
units.question: What is calculus in this context?
units.explanation: Calculus is the hardened deposit formed from plaque.
rationales: It is not a new enamel layer.

units.title: Locate gingival inflammation
units.lesson: Gingivitis describes inflammation of the gingiva. Redness, swelling and bleeding can be features; discomfort may be limited. Gingivitis and periodontitis should not be used as synonyms. A symptom by itself does not establish the extent of supporting-tissue destruction. Read clinical findings together rather than assigning disease severity from pain alone.
units.question: Which tissue is central to the term gingivitis?
units.explanation: Gingivitis names inflammation of the gingiva.
rationales: Pulp inflammation is a different concept.
This is not the periodontal tissue named.

units.title: Recognize destructive periodontal disease
units.lesson: Periodontitis involves destruction of supporting tissues around teeth, including bone. It differs from inflammation confined to the gingiva. Clinical attachment and supporting bone matter when describing disease extent. These concepts explain why appearance alone is incomplete; this chapter does not teach a self-diagnosis rule or choose treatment.
units.question: Which feature distinguishes destructive periodontal disease from gingival inflammation alone?
units.explanation: Loss of supporting tissues is the relevant distinction.
rationales: Colour alone does not establish destruction.

units.title: Separate stage from grade
units.lesson: Periodontal classification uses stage to summarize severity and management complexity, and grade to describe progression-related information and risk. These labels need a full assessment. Do not infer a patient’s stage or grade from one symptom or a single study card. For exams, first remember the different questions each label addresses.
units.question: Which pairing best matches stage and grade?
choices: Stage: favourite colour; grade: appointment time
Both mean exactly the same thing
units.explanation: Stage and grade summarize different disease dimensions.

units.question: Which statement avoids overinterpreting symptoms in gingivitis?
choices: Pain must be present in every case
Limited discomfort does not exclude gingival inflammation
Bleeding alone proves the extent of supporting bone loss
units.explanation: Gingivitis may cause limited discomfort; symptom presence alone does not quantify supporting-tissue destruction.
rationales: Pain is not mandatory in every case.
Bone loss cannot be quantified from bleeding alone.
units.hint: Do not turn one symptom into a universal rule.
